title: "A Man for Every Day" versus "Mighty Tight Woman"
summary: Reitz points to the contrast between two of her songs; Wallace says each came in a different year and mood.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Let me ask you something. When you sing, you know, you sing a song like "I'm a Mighty Tight Woman."
Yeah.
And you say, "Sweet papa, let me be your slave."
Yeah.
Then you turn around, listen to this now, and you sing another song, "I got a man for every day in the week."
Okay. Now those are two very different ideas.
Yeah, see I need a man every day in the
week one time, one year.
Yeah.
I made "Mighty Tight Woman" another year.
Yeah.
(Intelligible).
Well, what do you really believe? How about a man for every day in the week?
(Laughter.)
Give me a man for every day of the week.
You like it?
I wish I had a man for every day. I wish I had a man for one day of the week.
(Laughter.)
I like that idea very much.
What are you looking at me for?
I ain't looking at you.
You must be looking at me.
I ain't looking at you.
That's a song your grandma wrote and sang, "I Want a Man For Every Day in the Week." I love that song.
I say, "My Monday man, he buys my ."
Right.
"My Tuesday man don't ask me where I've been."
Right.
"My Wednesday man (unintelligible)" -- "I Want a Man For Every Day in the Week."
But that's a very different story than "Sweet papa, I want to be your slave."
Yeah, but that was one year. Yeah, but this year. I (unintelligible). __________, you go on home.
(Laughter.)
You're too young.
(Unintelligible).
